title: Virology Research Program
text: Approximately 20% of all cancers result from infectious agents, with the majority of these malignancies being virus-associated cancers. The Virology Program (VIR) focuses on deciphering the basic mechanisms by which human tumor viruses are linked to the development of malignancy. The long-term goal of VIR is to understand viral perturbation sufficiently to generate new therapies, including small molecules, biologics, and vaccines that target viruses and viral cancers. The aims for VIR are focused on five research areas. These include understanding: (i) Viruses and Immunity (ii) Virus-Cell Interactions (iii) Viral Pathogenesis and Tumorigenesis (iv) Cancers impacted by HIV infection, and (v) Clinical & Translational Virology, which includes gene therapy, immune therapy and global oncology. Recent discoveries include the finding that virus-infected cells secrete exosomes or extracellular vesicles, which modulate the tumor environment, and the discovery that viral- encoded microRNAs contribute to the development of neoplasms. Additional findings focus on the modulation of innate immune signaling pathways by oncogenic viruses, epigenetic modifications in the context of viral cancers, and development of new therapies for AIDS-associated cancers. There are 23 program members from 10 different departments across campus. These faculty investigators have 39 research grants and $9.7 million (direct costs) in annual extramural support including $2.4 million from NCI and $5.5 million from other peer and other NIH. Members authored a total of 407 cancer-relevant publications during the past 5 years; 13% were intra-programmatic, and 16% were inter-programmatic. VIR is the administrative home of LCCC viral vector/gene therapy efforts and based on overlapping biology is working closely with the Immunology (IMM) research program. LCCC’s humanized mouse program is led by Victor Garcia’s work in VIR. There are extremely accomplished investigators in VIR including Dr. Jack Griffith, elected to the National Academy of Sciences, Dr. Raab-Traub, National Cancer Advisory Board member, and Dr. Damania who serves on the NCI Board of Scientific Counselors. Research in VIR is informed by the Office of Community Outreach and Engagement particularly with respect to HPV-associated cancers with an emphasis on translational studies related to human papilloma virus (HPV) including recruitment of new faculty and investment of pilot funding. HPV-associated cervical and oral cancers are of particular interest to LCCC as the incidence of HPV- associated cervical and oral cancer in our catchment area exceeds the national average.

title: Genetic Predictors of Prostate Cancer Survival
text:
While prostate cancer screening reduces death from prostate cancer, it does so at the cost of unnecessary
treatment of men with nonaggressive disease. To address this, we propose to identify inherited genetic
changes that influence survival time after a diagnosis of prostate cancer and incorporating such genetic
information into prostate cancer screening tools. If successful, this will enable more precise prostate cancer
screening, reducing both death from prostate cancer and unnecessary treatment.

title: Programmable DNA Nanostructures as Biomedical and Structural Scaffolds
text:
DNA nanostructures have promise in biomedical applications such as biosensing, drug delivery and bioimaging,
but the field faces several challenges for it to be used in practical applications. In addressing these challenges,
I propose to develop robust, multifunctional drug delivery platform for treating multisystemic diseases and design
self-assembled 3D DNA crystals as scaffolds for X-ray structure determination using the new technique of Serial
Femtosecond X-ray Crystallography. In the long-term, I envision that our modular, platform technology using
DNA nanostructures can be adopted by other labs for different disease treatments and drug screening and to
obtain crystallographic information of hard-to-crystallize molecules.

title: Investigation of dopamine signaling pathways in medium spiny neurons
text:
Schizophrenia is a debilitating mental health disorder characterized by aberrant phasic dopamine
signaling in the striatum, and effective treatment with antipsychotics is limited by knowledge gaps in dopamine
physiology. There is evidence that dopamine is encoded by different postsynaptic pathways depending on the
type of release, but this has never been examined in the dorsolateral striatum or in the setting of
antipsychotics. This proposal aims to provide foundational knowledge for dopamine physiology and
schizophrenia treatment by (1) determining how postsynaptic pathways encode phasic dopamine release, and
(2) determining what postsynaptic pathways are antagonized by effective and ineffective antipsychotics upon
phasic dopamine release.

title: Enhancing anti-tumor immunotherapy with an engineered XCL1 protein
text:
Immunotherapy has shown promise in treating many forms of cancer. Significant side effects, large numbers of
patients resistant to common treatment modalities, and inability to effectively treat many solid cancers have
hindered immunotherapy success. The goal of this Phase I SBIR project is to show that our lead molecule
promotes anti-tumor immunity by selectively recruiting effector tumor killing cells to the tumor. Achievement of
Phase I milestones will pave the way for assembly of an investigational new drug application in Phase II.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-Mediated Therapeutic Targeting of CAG Repeats in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 12
text:
In spinocerebellar ataxia type 12 (SCA12), CRISPR/Cas9-mediated CAG repeat removal may be therapeutically
beneficial. Using genetically engineered human iPSC-derived extracellular vesicles, the Cas9 Ribonucleoprotein
(RNP) will be delivered into SCA12 knock-mouse and various sets of human isogenic control and SCA12 iPSC-
derived neurons, in order to rescue SCA12-related phenotypes.

title: The reninness score: integrative analysis of multi-omic data to define renin cell identity
text:
The goal of this project is to develop a computational tool to quantify and study the chromatin configuration and
transcriptional regulators characteristic of renin-expressing cells and renin recruitment process. By studying the
regulatory networks of renin recruitment, the proposed project will investigate potential therapeutic targets and
novel ways to diagnose and monitor treatment progression for kidney diseases, vascular diseases, and
hypertension.

title: A Versatile Chemical-Genetic Approach to Determine Bases for Arrhythmogenesis and Sodium Channelopathies
text:
The goal of this project is to apply chemical genetics to examine the basis for cardiovascular disease and
deepen the understanding of diverse physiological roles of the cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel.

title: Mentoring program in patient-oriented research in microbial genomics
text:
The overall goals of this program are to provide an outstanding training program in mentored patient-oriented
research in antimicrobial resistance and microbial genomics by examining the gut microbiome is a reservoir for
antibiotic resistance, as well as for pathobionts that can cause non-infectious chronic disease complications.
This will be achieved through rigorous projects that will assess microbial factors that predict colonization and
clearance of MDROs and progression to systemic infection and non-infectious complications such as rejection,
taking advantage of high-resolution sequencing data. We will use rigorous machine learning analysis to obtain
a detailed understanding of gut microbiome risk factors, which will inform predictive risk management algorithms
to aid in critical clinical decision-making for MDRO colonization in high-risk patients.

title: Ultra low-input epigenetic sequencing with combined enzymatic and long-read technologies
text:
Modifications to individual nucleobases in DNA play a crucial role in human development and human diseases.
Our project aims to address the limitations faced by the current genomic tools through the creation of new non-
destructive sequencing technologies that can localize the major modifications to DNA that shape gene
expression. This advancement will empower researchers to study DNA more comprehensively, even with low
input materials, and will thus be broadly applicable to different biological and biomedical questions.

title: Stretching their Reach: Robotic Support for Older Individuals with Mild Cognitive Impairment and Early Alzheimer's Dementia
text:
Assistive robots have the potential to enhance individual autonomy, reduce human burden, and lower
healthcare costs associated with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and mild dementia while supporting their
professional caregivers (CareStaff) and care partners (Carers). StretchTM is a mobile manipulator robot
designed to support everyday activities through a lightweight telescoping arm mounted on a mobile base, using
artificial intelligence and voice prompts. Our research will develop and evaluate how Stretch can provide
support to older adults with MCI/Mild Dementia, Carers, and CareStaff, across three key application areas
(cognitive assistance, social engagement, and safety management).

title: Preventing follicular lymphoma progression and transformation through precision therapy
text:
Follicular lymphomas are characterized by translocations in BCL2 and somatic mutations of epigenetic modifier
genes such as EZH2. In germinal centers mutant EZH2 epigenetically reprograms B-cells to form an aberrant
immunological niche. Understanding how EZH2 mutant follicular lymphomas survive in their unique rich
microenvironment will advance our knowledge of the underlying mechanisms by which EZH2 mutations drive
lymphomagenesis and inform the design and preclinical development of new treatment strategies to prevent
disease progression and transformation.

title: Evaluation of digital ischemia in scleroderma with multiparametric MRI
text:
We present here a novel magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) based imaging approach for a comprehensive
quantitative assessment of vasculopathy, tissue hypoxia, and fibrosis in the hands of patients with scleroderma.
The short-term goal of this project is to identify effective imaging biomarkers to guide prevention and to monitor
effectiveness of therapy for digital ulcers in patients with scleroderma. The potential future implication of this
study is the development of peripheral vascular imaging tools that could be applied to patients with other
autoimmune rheumatic disease conditions or peripheral artery disease.

title: Mechanisms of epigenetic memory in human cells
text:
Almost every cell in an individual has the same DNA sequence yet vary greatly in the chemical modifications on
DNA called epigenetics that can give rise to different cell types. Failure to regulate the epigenetic content of
human cells is a hallmark of aging, cancer cells, and many human diseases. My research aims to understand
how epigenetic modifications are established on the human genome and to understand how aberrant epigenetic
patterns in human DNA can lead to disease states.

title: Metabolic targeting of CD4 T cells in CNS autoimmunity
text:
Because one of the key drivers of multiple sclerosis (MS) is over-active inflammatory immune cells entering the
brain, immunosuppressive therapies can decrease relapses in MS; unfortunately, the benefits of general
immunosuppressive therapies on disease progression are not sufficiently sustained over years and risk
targeting cells needed to fight infections and help us heal. We have shown that by targeting methionine
metabolism—either by restricting methionine in the diet or by inhibiting an enzyme (MAT2A) that metabolizes
methionine—we can limit the number of disease-driving immune cells in the brain and thus slow disease
severity in a mouse model of MS. Understanding how these interventions work to reduceand potentially
blockMS pathology, whether these interventions also affect normal immune cell function, and if the
intervention can reverse active disease will potentially uncover new treatment avenues for autoimmune
diseases such as MS.

title: Adrenal Origins of Aldosterone Excess
text:
Primary aldosteronism (PA) – the most common cause of endocrine hypertension – leads to cardiovascular
damage and enhanced potential for metabolic syndrome. Recently, using pathologic adrenal tissue from patients
with PA, we identified somatic mutations that cause clonal expansion of autonomous aldosterone-producing
adrenal cortical cells. These findings form the foundation for this competing renewal application submission that
will test two hypotheses: i) PA initiates with adrenocortical cell somatic gene mutations that dysregulate
intracellular calcium signaling leading to autonomous aldosterone production (Aim 1); and, ii) the amount of
excess aldosterone produced in PA is determined by transcriptional regulation of the genes harboring
aldosterone-driver somatic mutations (Aim 2).

title: Small Animal Cancer Imaging
text: SMALL ANIMAL CANCER IMAGING (SACI) SHARED RESOURCE: PROJECT SUMMARY With the revolution in molecular biology, transgenic animal models – in particular mice – have become an indispensable part of the cancer research armamentarium. The Siteman Cancer Center’s (SCC) Small Animal Cancer Imaging (SACI) Shared Resource (SR) (initially established under the auspices of the NCI’s Small Animal Imaging Resource Program) addresses the need for nondestructive imaging and analysis of small animal laboratory models of cancer. It provides state-of-the-art facilities and infrastructure for magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography, X-ray computed tomography, single-photon emission computed tomography, and optical (including Cerenkov) imaging of mice, rats, and other small laboratory animals that serve as models of cancer. SACI combines instrumental and intellectual capabilities found at few other institutions and serves a broad community of cancer scientists who have a pressing need for quantitative image analysis of small animal model systems. The principal functions of SACI are to provide SCC members: i) access to, and maintenance of, small animal magnetic resonance, nuclear medicine, and optical imaging scanners for cancer research; ii) technology expertise and consultation in study design, protocol development, and data analysis/interpretation. In addition to supporting cancer research applications of small animal imaging, SACI also provides research and development at the frontier of imaging technology in an effort to make the most powerful new imaging strategies available to its community of users. The SR is organized around three modality-specific imaging components: (i) nuclear medicine, (ii) magnetic resonance, and (iii) optical. An overarching goal is translation to the clinic of imaging protocols and therapeutic agents developed and validated with small animal models. Thus, SACI directly supports the mission of the SCC by supporting basic discovery cancer research and cancer imaging protocols with translational potential.

title: Acquisition of a Bruker timsTOF Ultra 2 to Advance Clinical and Translational Proteomics at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia
text: Recent advances in clinical proteomics are revolutionizing how we diagnose, monitor, and study human disease. This proposal seeks to acquire a state-of-the-art mass spectrometer to enable NIH-funded investigators to apply powerful approaches, such as biofluid proteomics, immunopeptidomes, and low-input sample analysis, to complex conditions like cancer, heart disease, and rare pediatric syndromes. The resulting insights will help improve diagnostics, uncover new therapeutic targets, and drive progress in precision medicine.

title: Type I interferon Impacts Treatment Response in Rheumatoid Arthritis
text:
Study Title: Type I Interferon Impacts Treatment Response in Rheumatoid Arthritis
PROJECT NARRATIVE
Insufficient treatment in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) results in increased morbidity and mortality, and a heavy
economic burden associated with loss of function. This research will help to develop a more individualized
approach to therapy in RA and determine an immunologic basis of non-response to TNF inhibitors. The findings could
suggest a molecular rationale for the use of specific therapies in biologically defined subgroups of patients.

title: Functional characterization of Chlamydia trachomatis inclusion membrane proteins and their role in subversion of the host vesicular trafficking
text:
Chlamydia trachomatis is the leading cause of bacterial sexually transmitted infections and can result in severe
complications, including pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility. Despite its significant
clinical impact, the mechanisms by which C. trachomatis manipulates host cellular pathways remain poorly
understood. This renewal focuses on elucidating how the C. trachomatis Inc proteins CT229 and IncC coordinate
interactions with host and bacterial factors to regulate vesicle fusion, maintain inclusion stability, and evade
immune defenses, ultimately providing critical insights for the development of novel therapeutic strategies.
